rows.source: HSE respiratory-protective-equipment guidance
rows.verified: RPE used at work must be adequate and provide effective protection.

rows.source: HSE respiratory-protective-equipment guidance
rows.verified: RPE must be suitable for the intended use and matched to the wearer, task and working environment.

rows.source: HSE respiratory-protective-equipment guidance
rows.verified: RPE must be selected, used and maintained by properly trained people.

rows.source: HSE respiratory-protective-equipment guidance
rows.verified: RPE must be correctly maintained, examined, tested and stored.

rows.source: HSE respiratory-protective-equipment guidance
rows.verified: Records should be kept for RPE selection, maintenance and testing.

rows.source: HSE respiratory-protective-equipment guidance
rows.verified: RPE is a last line of protection and should be used after other reasonably practicable controls have been taken.

rows.source: HSE respiratory-protective-equipment guidance
rows.verified: Tight-fitting facepieces require fit testing, and each type worn by an employee should be fit tested.

rows.source: HSE respiratory-protective-equipment guidance
rows.verified: Facial hair prevents a reliable seal for tight-fitting masks; alternative RPE that does not rely on a tight face seal may be needed.

rows.source: HSE respiratory-protective-equipment guidance
rows.verified: RPE protection depends on contaminant type and concentration, required protection factor, face fit, compatibility, training, maintenance, filter condition and work rate.

rows.source: HSE respiratory-protective-equipment guidance
rows.verified: General RPE evidence or a successful fit test does not prove exposure is controlled in every task or establish an exact parcel-level health probability.

rows.source: HSE Control of Lead at Work guidance
rows.verified: Employers must prevent exposure to lead or, where this is not reasonably practicable, control employee exposure.

rows.source: HSE Control of Lead at Work guidance
rows.verified: Lead exposure can affect the blood, nervous system, kidneys and reproductive function.

rows.source: HSE Control of Lead at Work guidance
rows.verified: Workers can absorb lead by breathing dust, fume or vapour or by swallowing contamination.

rows.source: HSE Control of Lead at Work guidance
rows.verified: Employers should reduce the number of people exposed, the amount of lead and the duration of exposure.

rows.source: HSE Control of Lead at Work guidance
rows.verified: Mechanical, administrative and behavioural controls must be kept in good working order and used when needed.

rows.source: HSE Control of Lead at Work guidance
rows.verified: Medical surveillance should be discussed with an appointed doctor and supported by good records.

rows.source: HSE Control of Lead at Work guidance
rows.verified: Workers and supervisors need training on hazards, dust controls, equipment cleaning, PPE, emergencies and personal hygiene.

rows.source: HSE Control of Lead at Work guidance
rows.verified: Significant exposure includes atmospheric exposure above half the occupational exposure limit, substantial ingestion risk or skin exposure to absorbable lead compounds.

rows.source: HSE Control of Lead at Work guidance
rows.verified: Lead risk depends on lead form, process, air concentration, ingestion and skin routes, duration, hygiene, control performance and medical-surveillance findings.

rows.source: HSE Control of Lead at Work guidance
rows.verified: General lead guidance does not prove contamination, blood-lead status or an exact exposure probability at an individual parcel.
